links.title: Cardano Leios - Voting
links.tooltip: Vote decisions and certification margin for the same window

panels.title: Fetch bandwidth — how much of what we pulled was worth pulling

panels.description: EB body bytes split by what became of them. Good is bytes that ended up used. Invalid failed validation, evicted arrived but was dropped before use, extra was fetched beyond what was needed. These are node metrics rather than log-derived, so they survive any tracer severity change.
panels.title: EB body fetch bytes by outcome

panels.description: The same split for transaction fetches. Read alongside the body panel: a body path that looks healthy while the tx path wastes bytes points at the tx cache rather than at diffusion.
panels.title: Tx fetch bytes by outcome

panels.description: Share of fetched bytes that did not end up used, per node. A node consistently above its peers is fetching from somewhere that keeps losing the race, or re-fetching what it already had. Denominator guarded so a quiet node reads as no data rather than as a spike.
panels.title: Wasted fetch bytes, share of all bytes fetched

panels.description:
Bytes a node took in over the bytes its fetch scheduler asked for, per node. The two come from independent sources, a node metric and the scheduler's own decision trace, so this doubles as a consistency check on both.

Around 1 is healthy. Persistently below means requests going unfulfilled, which points at peers not delivering rather than at the scheduler. Above means more arrived than was asked for, and should corroborate as extra or evicted bytes on the panel to the left.

Only hosts running leios_diffusion_process have the denominator, so a host without it shows no series here rather than skewing a fleet figure. Denominators are guarded, so an idle node reads as no data.
panels.title: Delivered against requested bytes
Fetch scheduler — is it keeping up, and is there anything to fetch

panels.description:
Bodies a node still wants against offers its peers have advertised, per node. Read them together: missing bodies rising while offers stay flat is diffusion failing to reach that node, missing bodies rising with offers is its scheduler falling behind. Narrow with the instance variable.

Each node carries its own view of this, so the series are per node rather than a fleet total.

EBs tracked is context for how much work is queued rather than part of that comparison, and it runs orders of magnitude above the pair, so it is drawn unfilled and thin to keep the two readable. It also must not be stacked with them: a body can only be missing for an EB that is tracked, so missing bodies is a subset of tracked and stacking nested series counts the same EBs twice.

The gauges expire five minutes after a node stops reporting fetch decisions, so a gap means its pipeline went quiet rather than a value holding steady. During a load generator idle period that is every node at once.
panels.title: Missing bodies against offers held

panels.description: Requests outstanding and how many peers they are spread across. A high inflight total on few peers is concentration, which makes body arrival hostage to one link.
panels.title: Requests in flight and peers carrying them

panels.description: How long a decision round takes. A round is meant to be cheap; the failure worth catching is it becoming a brake on the fetch loop, so watch p99 rather than the median.
panels.title: Fetch decision round duration

panels.description: Work the scheduler issued, as rates. Body requests are the subset that pull EB bodies; jobs are the units of work created to service them.
panels.title: Fetch request and job rate
Tx cache — what it spared, measured at two points

panels.description: Measured at body acquisition: the share of an EB's transactions that still needed full validation once the body arrived. Lower is better. This is the LeiosBodyHits view, and it is a different question from the vote-time panel beside it — this one is about what the cache held when the body landed.
panels.title: Needed full validation at body acquisition

panels.description: Measured at vote time: the share of an EB's transactions reapplied from the cache rather than fully applied. Higher is better. This is the LeiosEbValidated view and it is the same quantity the throughput dashboard computes in LogQL, here as a counter ratio instead.
panels.title: Cache hit rate at vote time

panels.description: How full the tx cache is. If load sits at capacity while the validation share above is climbing, the cache is being evicted faster than it is being used and wants sizing.
panels.title: Tx cache load and size

panels.description:
The share of an EB's transactions the LeiosTxCache path handled, and where they dropped out. Nested rather than a partition: the source states txsInEb >= tracked >= acquired >= validated, so each line sits at or below the one above and they must never cross.

These are not expected to approach 100%. Most of an EB's transactions are already in the node's mempool by the time the body arrives, so the cache path only ever accounts for the remainder; tracked reaching txsInEb would mean the mempool had failed to have them. Coverage is the panel to the right.

The three sitting exactly on top of each other is the healthy reading: everything tracked was acquired and everything acquired was validated, so there is no attrition. Divergence between them is the signal.

Shown as shares because the underlying counts are summed across nodes that each process the same transactions, so their absolute volume is not a network rate. Denominators guarded, so an idle node reads as no data.
panels.title: EB transaction funnel, share via the cache path

panels.description:
Where an EB's transactions were found when the body arrived: already in the mempool, or in neither the cache nor the mempool.

The hit rate on the right axis is (txsInEb - missedBoth) / txsInEb, the formula the source gives. It answers a different question from the validation share on the stat above: that one asks how many transactions needed full validation, this one asks how many the node had never seen at all, and the two differ by about an order of magnitude.

These counts and the funnel beside them measure overlapping populations and must not be added together. Denominator guarded, so an idle node reads as no data.
panels.title: Cache and mempool coverage

panels.description: Announcements relayed to us by upstream peers, before deduplication, per node. Compare against the deduplicated LeiosAnnouncementAccepted rate on the voting dashboard: the ratio of the two is announcement fan-in.
panels.title: Peer announcement relay rate

panels.description: Announcements flagged as equivocating: a peer announcing a second, different EB for an election it already announced. Expected to sit flat at zero. Anything sustained is either a faulty node or a deliberate one, and this is the only view of it.
panels.title: Equivocating announcements
Diffusion timing — when the body and its tx closure actually landed

panels.description:
How long diffusion took, from the EB's slot to the moment the node had the data. Body is the EB body download completing; closure is the last referenced transaction arriving, so it is never earlier than the body. The gap between the two curves is what the tx fetch path costs on top of the body.

Both kinds report the latency already computed, as bodyAgeSeconds and closureAgeSeconds, so these are histograms over a reported field rather than a timestamp join across streams.
panels.title: EB body and tx closure age percentiles

panels.description:
Share of tx closures complete within each age, read straight off the histogram buckets rather than from a quantile, so it answers how often diffusion beat a deadline rather than where the median sits.

A closure arriving late is a vote not cast, so a falling 2s or 3s share is the shape to watch. Thresholds are bucket boundaries, matched on le as an exact string. alloy renders a whole-number bound with its decimal, so the bound 2.0 is le="2.0" and le="2" would match nothing and plot an empty series. Changing a threshold means changing the buckets in leios_diffusion_process and writing the bound here the same way it appears there.
panels.title: Tx closure complete within deadline

panels.description:
How long an EB announcement takes to reach a node, from the announcementAgeSeconds the receiver records. Per-node percentiles then averaged, so one busy node cannot dominate the line — the same reading the retired Loki panel gave, from a histogram that survives Loki retention.

Late announcements convert directly into chainTipDoesNotAnnounce declines, so this is the leading indicator for that reason code on the voting dashboard.
panels.title: Announcement age, mean of per-node percentiles
EB announcement delay CDF
panels.description: Fraction of EB announcements arriving within each bucket. Late announcements convert directly into chainTipDoesNotAnnounce declines, since a voter whose tip has not adopted the announcing RB cannot vote when its window opens. Read the low buckets against lVoteWindowSlots for the network in question.

panels.title: Late EB announcements
panels.description: Rate of announcements the node considered late, per minute. Pairs with the CDF above: the CDF says how bad the tail is, this says how often it bites. Grafana shows a PromQL lint info here which is expected, due to the cardano-node _counter suffix convention rather than _total.

panels.title: EB announcement age by producer
panels.description: How long each producing pool EB announcements take to reach our nodes, from the announcementAgeSeconds field the receiving node records. This is the one view here that measures other operators directly rather than inferring them from votes. A pool whose median sits beyond the vote window cannot have its EBs voted on in time no matter what we do, so a high value here is that operator problem, not ours. Sorted slowest first. The trace count is one line per receiving node rather than per EB, so it scales with how many nodes are reporting and is a relative volume indicator, not an EB count. Live diffusion only: chain-sync discoveries are minutes old by nature and are excluded.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.5, {kind="LeiosAnnouncementAccepted", instance=~"$instance"} | json pool="electionPool",age="announcementAgeSeconds",src="source" | src="receivedViaLeiosNotify" | unwrap age [$__range]) by (pool)

quantile_over_time(0.9, {kind="LeiosAnnouncementAccepted", instance=~"$instance"} | json pool="electionPool",age="announcementAgeSeconds",src="source" | src="receivedViaLeiosNotify" | unwrap age [$__range]) by (pool)
sum by (pool) (count_over_time({kind="LeiosAnnouncementAccepted", instance=~"$instance"} | json pool="electionPool",src="source" | src="receivedViaLeiosNotify" [$__range]))

panels.description:
The largest age actually observed, which the histograms cannot report: histogram_quantile is capped at the top finite bucket, so an outlier beyond it reads as that bound and disappears. These gauges carry the last observed value per node, so max_over_time recovers a real peak.

They sample rather than record: these kinds arrive at a rate comparable to the scrape interval, so a given spike can fall between scrapes. Read them for tail behaviour over a window, not as a guarantee about any single EB.
panels.title: Peak age reached — true maxima from the last-value gauges
Tx closure age distribution
panels.description:
Every closure completion bucketed, rather than reduced to percentiles. This is the panel that shows shape: percentile lines average away a split population, so a fleet where local peers land fast and remote ones land slow reads as one healthy middle. Two bands here and a p50 sitting between them is that case.

Closure rather than body because closure is what gates a vote: the body alone is not enough to validate an EB.

Cell values are observations per second rather than counts, because the buckets are read as a rate and differenced against the bucket below. Multiply by 60 for closures per minute, so 0.0167 is one per minute. A small decimal is expected and is not a sign of missing data.

How many upstream peers relayed each EB announcement at one node. LeiosPeerAnnouncement is emitted once per peer per newly counted announcement, so the count per ebHash is that node's fan-in. Pick the node with the variable.

One node at a time because fan-in is per node: grouping by ebHash across every instance exceeds Loki's 500 series limit, and summing across them would report fleet-wide relay events as though they were a single node's fan-in.

The only Loki panel here, so the row is collapsed by default and the query is instant rather than ranged. topk bounds the result, and an instant query only merges into a single frame in a table, not a timeseries.

targets.expr: topk(25, sum by (ebHash) (count_over_time({kind="LeiosPeerAnnouncement", instance="$fanInInstance"} | json ebHash="ebHash" [$__range])))

panels.title: Announcement fan-in — distinct peers per EB (expensive, Loki)

list.description: Single node for the announcement fan-in panel. Fan-in is a per-node quantity and grouping by ebHash across every instance exceeds Loki's series limit, so that panel picks one node rather than aggregating. Scoped to instances actually emitting LeiosPeerAnnouncement.
list.name: fanInInstance
